title: From Machine Learning to Large-Scale EO Products
text:
Welcome
The past decade has seen a rapid expansion in the production of large-scale geospatial products derived from Earth observation (EO) data using machine learning (ML). This website is the result of bringing together map-makers across the EO and ML communities. It presents an end-to-end account of the good practices, challenges, and common pitfalls that span the entire pipeline from raw satellite data to a published, validated map product, and treats that pipeline as an integrated workflow rather than a sequence of independent steps. The focus is on wall-to-wall raster maps at moderate resolution (10–30 m) and continental to global extent, produced with ML from open satellite archives, mainly Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2 and Landsat.
We organize the discussion around six interconnected themes which trace the pipeline from the EO data landscape and preprocessing, through ML-specific stages of dataset construction, model design, and training, to uncertainty quantification, map generation, dissemination, and validation.

title: From Machine Learning to Large-Scale EO Products
text:
Main Sections
Overview of the EO data infrastructure landscape — Satellite missions, data access platforms, and the practical trade-offs of working with petabyte-scale archives.
Data selection and preprocessing — Temporal strategies, cloud masking, SAR preprocessing, and the hidden choices that shape the training signal.
ML dataset construction and model training — Data formats, spatial splitting, gridding, model design, and training considerations specific to EO.
Uncertainty quantification — Sources of uncertainty, quantification methods, calibration diagnostics, and how to operationalize uncertainty in map products.
Map production and distribution — Tiled inference at scale, artifact mitigation, post-processing, and cloud-native dissemination.
Validation — Design-based accuracy assessment, the distinction between model evaluation and map validation, and reporting standards.

title: How to Use This Book
text:
Overview
This book presents an end-to-end account of good practices for producing large-scale geospatial products from Earth observation data using machine learning. It is organized around six interconnected themes that trace the pipeline from raw satellite data to a published, validated map product. Each chapter can be read independently or as part of the full pipeline.

title: How to Use This Book
text:
Structure
The book is divided into the following parts:
Overview of the EO data infrastructure landscape covers the satellite missions and data access platforms available to practitioners, and the practical trade-offs involved in choosing between them.
Data selection and preprocessing addresses how to select which observations to include and how to process them into analysis-ready formats, covering both optical and SAR data.
Machine learning dataset construction and model training discusses data formats, spatial splitting strategies, gridding choices, and model design considerations specific to EO data.
Uncertainty quantification surveys sources of uncertainty in EO-derived maps and methods for quantifying, calibrating, and operationalizing uncertainty estimates.
Map production and distribution covers the engineering challenges of tiled inference at scale, post-processing, and dissemination in cloud-native formats.
Validation distinguishes model evaluation from map validation and presents design-based accuracy assessment and complementary validation approaches.

title: Introduction
text:
Maps, of varying scales and extents, are accessible and powerful tools for policy-makers and other stakeholders to visualize spatial patterns, and inform planning and decision making. Forest carbon claims made under the UNFCCC REDD+ mechanism rest on mapped estimates of extent and change [1]. The humanitarian sector relies on rapidly generated maps to assess damage extent [2], and on population maps to determine which communities are at risk [3].
The past decade has seen a rapid expansion in the production of large-scale geospatial products derived from Earth observation (EO) data using machine learning (ML). Driven by expanding model capacity and compute availability, the domain has reached a level of operational maturity where practitioners can routinely generate high-resolution global products, including maps of building footprints [4], land cover [5], canopy height [6], [7], renewable energy installations [8] and flood inundation [9]. The traditional EO toolkit (spectral indices, radiative transfer and other physical models, spectral unmixing, and classical ML pipelines built on hand-crafted features) historically delivered maps by leveraging locally calibrated models tuned to specific regions, sensors, or biomes; global products created this way were mosaics of local solutions. Deep learning has expanded the paradigm toward singular, globally applicable models trained on heterogeneous data, promising consistent worldwide products but also introducing challenges with no clear analog in the traditional workflow. Scaled inference, for instance, now demands specific engineering skills (distributed compute, efficient I/O, cloud-native data formats) that traditional EO scientists rarely needed in the past. At the same time, the apparent ease with which such maps seem to be produced hides the complexity of the underlying pipeline, and the lowered barrier to entry has enabled a proliferation of map products released without adequate validation. Crucially, “maps are being developed by different organizations across the research-policy-practice interface, […] without a shared understanding of best practices” [10].
When considering the full workflow for a global map, every stage of the process presents domain-specific, tightly coupled challenges that have no direct equivalent in conventional machine learning. The failures we most often see in published maps are not failures of any single stage in isolation, but rather mismatches; e.g., train/test splits that rely on Sentinel-2 tile grids, introducing spatial overlap and hidden data leakage. Most reviews and tutorials on ML for EO are organized around methods or applications [11], [12], [13], [14]. Individual stages have received dedicated attention [15], [16], [17], [18], but a comprehensive account of the workflow as a whole is lacking, particularly for the steps between a trained model and a released product.
This article is addressed to a broad audience of researchers and practitioners, from those just entering the EO domain to ML experts looking to build ML-ready EO datasets or generate large-scale maps. It presents an end-to-end account of the good practices, challenges, and common pitfalls that span the entire pipeline, from the collection of satellite data to a published, validated map product. Throughout the article, we refer to many published products; two of them act as a common thread. WorldCereal [19] is an operational, categorical cropland and crop-type mapping system: it consumes per-pixel multi-sensor time series, classifies each pixel independently with gradient-boosted trees, runs inference on CPU, releases its 2021 products through Zenodo and Earth Engine, and validates its cropland layer through design-based accuracy assessment against a probability sample. Canopy height map (CHM) refers to ECHOSAT [20], the most recent of three canopy height maps from the same group; where ECHOSAT leaves a step undocumented, we take it from its predecessors [21], [22]. It is a research-oriented continuous regression product: it consumes multi-temporal image patches, is trained on GPU with encoder–decoder networks, is released through Earth Engine, and is evaluated against its own test set. We contrast their choices in boxes throughout the article.
It would be misleading to present map-making sequentially: acquire, preprocess, train, infer, validate, publish. Several constraints run backwards through the workflow. For example, to minimize domain shift, training data preparation should ideally align with the data sources and processing baselines available on the global inference platform. As such, Figure 1.1 presents the workflow as a directed graph, emphasizing that choices made at each stage carry consequences for other ones, and awareness of these dependencies is one of the factors that separate a technically sound map from a misleading one.






Figure 1.1: The mapping workflow as a constraint network. Solid arrows are the familiar forward flow; dotted arrows indicate that every stage is conditioned by the intended map product. Dashed arrows are constraints that run backwards through the workflow, and are responsible for the most expensive and least recoverable mistakes in large-scale mapping: the training and inference data must match, or the model meets a distribution shift at deployment that it was never tested on; data must be acquired over the regions where validation is intended, since without inference there, there is nothing to validate against; the uncertainty the product has to report constrains which models are admissible; the compute budget available for deployment shapes model development; and the validation regions must be excluded from the training and model-selection sets. The section numbers in the boxes refer to the parts of this book: § II = EO data landscape, § III = Data selection & preprocessing, § IV = ML dataset & training, § V = Uncertainty quantification, § VI = Map production & distribution, § VII = Validation.

title: Overview of the EO data infrastructure landscape
text:
Researchers and practitioners must navigate a complex and rapidly evolving ecosystem of satellite data sources and access platforms. The choices made in the early stages (which mission to use, which processing level to start from, and which platform to retrieve the data through) have downstream consequences that are easy to underestimate. This section maps the landscape of available EO data, and discusses the practical considerations of accessing them.






NoteDefinition · Processing levels, analysis-ready, ML-ready



Processing levels. How far a product is from the raw signal. Level 0 is unprocessed instrument data; Level 1 adds time referencing, calibration and geolocation (e.g., Sentinel-1 GRD, Sentinel-2 L1C top-of-atmosphere reflectance); Level 2 holds geophysical variables at the resolution and location of the Level 1 source (e.g., Sentinel-2 L2A surface reflectance, Landsat Collection 2 Level-2); Level 3 maps variables onto a uniform space-time grid, often by compositing (e.g., the Sentinel-1 monthly mosaics) [1].
Analysis-ready data (ARD). Data processed to standardized physical specifications (calibrated, geometrically orthorectified, radiometrically corrected, with per-pixel quality masks and documented provenance) so that it can be used for analysis with a minimum of additional user effort.
ML-ready. Data formatted into standardized tensors (e.g., spatial or temporal patches) and organized in high-throughput layouts to optimize I/O performance during model training.
While institutional standards (e.g., NASA, ESIP) often use AI-ready as a broader term encompassing FAIR metadata, licensing, and documentation, ML-ready specifically denotes the structural formatting required for efficient GPU ingestion.






[1] NASA Earthdata, “Data processing levels.” https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/learn/earth-observation-data-basics/data-processing-levels.

title: Accessing EO data
text:
The EO data access landscape has expanded significantly in recent years, but it is also fast-moving and not cleanly delineated: providers and platforms regularly restructure their offerings, pricing, and access policies, and the boundaries between “canonical provider”, “cloud re-distributor”, and “compute platform” are increasingly blurred. A unifying constraint across this landscape is data gravity: modern EO archives have grown to a scale where even freely available data is often impractical to move, and the position of compute relative to data has become a primary design factor. This is the reason some large-scale EO workflows today rely on platforms that co-locate data and compute instead of directly downloading from canonical providers.
Canonical EO data providers maintain authoritative archives of specific satellite missions and datasets. The Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (CDSE) serves as the primary distribution point for Sentinel missions and related European products, while also providing access to Copernicus Contributing Missions (CCM) to complement core open collections with commercial and national high-resolution imagery. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) provides access to Landsat observations. NASA Earthdata hosts MODIS, GEDI, ICESat-2, and other NASA Earth science products. The European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (EUMETSAT) distributes data from MSG, MTG, Sentinel-3, Sentinel-6, and related systems. The Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) offers NISAR, the ERS, JERS-1 and RADARSAT-1 legacy missions, and terrain-corrected Sentinel-1 products. Additional canonical providers include the JAXA Earth Observation Center for ALOS PALSAR, DLR Geoservice for TanDEM-X, and various other agencies maintaining specialized datasets on dedicated platforms.
Re-distribution platforms have emerged to simplify this access, though their roles vary considerably. Google Earth Engine (GEE) [1] is best understood as a compute ecosystem with co-located data rather than a pure data provider. Access is primarily through server-side operations and the platform is highly effective for tasks that exploit this paradigm, including extracting moderate-scale ML training datasets, a common use in the community. However, large-scale data extraction is not what GEE is built for, and users quickly run into export quotas and rate limits on the free and non-commercial tiers. While commercial tiers relax these limits, bulk exports require routing through Google Cloud Storage and incur significant egress fees. This presents a key structural barrier for academic and open-science teams, who produce the vast majority of public EO benchmark datasets, as few research budgets can accommodate high-throughput cloud infrastructure and egress costs. Microsoft Planetary Computer (MPC), by contrast, is essentially a data access layer: a STAC catalog of cloud-hosted Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) in Azure Blob Storage, with no built-in server-side processing since the retirement of its free compute environment in mid-20241. Amazon Web Services (AWS) Simple Storage Service (S3) hosts EO data on both free buckets (e.g., Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF collections for Sentinel-2 L2A and Landsat 8/9 via the AWS Open Data Program) and requester-pays buckets (e.g., the primary USGS Landsat Collection 2 archive or complete Sentinel-2 SAFE zips, imposing transfer costs directly on the user). Additional platforms include Sentinel Hub, Google Cloud Storage public datasets, and CloudFerro2. Relying on re-distribution platforms introduces several trade-offs. Since these platforms ingest data from canonical EO providers, there may be latency between acquisition and availability, and their processing pipelines may differ from those of the original providers. As an example, we provide an overview of the processing differences between the native Sentinel-1/2 data products and their GEE equivalents in Appendix: Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 processing across access pathways. Data gaps can also occur, as regularly reported by users on the MPC GitHub repository.
Accessing EO data therefore involves practical choices across multiple dimensions. Each platform offers distinct trade-offs in where the data is hosted, support for server-side operations, suitability for large-scale download, and feasibility of running large-scale co-located compute; we summarize them in Table 3.1. A practical pattern that follows from data gravity is to treat EO data access as a two-stage process. Model development typically involves modest data volumes that can be downloaded comfortably from almost any provider; here, convenience and catalog coverage dominate the choice. Inference at scale, on the other hand, is dominated by data movement: pulling petabyte-scale imagery from one provider into a different compute environment is rarely tractable. As a result, practitioners typically either (i) co-locate inference compute with the data, or (ii) accept the time and storage cost of moving the EO data into their compute environment. Co-location only helps if the compute you need is available where the data is: large GPU pools are a hyperscaler feature, so GPU-bound inference is restricted to data hosted on AWS, Azure or GCP; CPU-bound pipelines have more options. The platform that minimizes friction for training is therefore often not the one that minimizes cost for inference, and moving between them introduces a risk of distribution shift that should not be taken lightly. No universally optimal solution exists: the most appropriate choice depends on the scale of analysis, computational requirements, institutional constraints, the practical cost of download and storage, and the acceptable trade-off between immediate convenience and the risk of lock-in to proprietary platforms.

title: Data selection and preprocessing
text: The quality of any ML-derived map is bounded by the quality of the data that feeds it. This section addresses the two foundational stages of the data pipeline: selecting which observations to include, and processing them into a form suitable for analysis. Data selection (see Data selection) involves navigating trade-offs between spatial coverage, temporal density, and data quality. These decisions are particularly consequential when working with global-scale EO archives where gaps, overlaps, and redundancies must all be managed explicitly. Data preprocessing (see Data preprocessing) covers the transformation of sensor measurements into analysis-ready data, a step whose apparent simplicity conceals a number of subtleties. Throughout, we emphasize that these choices are not neutral: they encode assumptions that propagate into the training signal and ultimately shape the reliability of the final product.

title: Data selection
text:
Temporal distribution
Selecting which observations to include requires navigating two interrelated concerns: the temporal distribution of acquisitions (Temporal distribution) and the quality criteria for both optical (Optical data selection) and SAR data (SAR data selection). They involve trade-offs that are straightforward to state but difficult to resolve in practice, particularly at global scale.
We frame the present discussion around the task of producing a yearly map, a common context, which also requires addressing the challenge of temporal data selection. Under this setting, we discuss how to select EO data in the temporal dimension within a period of approximately 12 months. The conclusions can be extended to shorter or longer windows of time, depending on the nature of the underlying feature being mapped. Furthermore, this framing assumes that multiple temporal acquisitions are available; this might not be the case for high- and very-high-resolution sensors: the Maxar mosaic used by Tolan et al. [1] and the SPOT mosaic underlying Schwartz et al. [2] each rest on a single acquisition per location. Two questions emerge: how observations are represented in time, and what time range they are drawn from.
Regarding representation, the first decision is whether the model sees observations at their original acquisition timestamps, or aggregated onto a fixed temporal grid. Three broad strategies emerge: single time-steps, time-series, or composites, each with its own trade-offs. Time-series are arguably the richest option, capturing phenomena like seasonal variation across a defined period. Pauls et al. [3] showed that a one-year time-series made of the least cloudy Sentinel-2 observation per month preserved the seasonal nuances and geolocation shifts that median composites tend to wash away, and Dixon et al. [4] found benefits in using a time-series of composited PlanetScope imagery over using a single image. The trade-off is data size and model capacity: they are memory-intensive to store by nature, and require a model handling temporal patterns. Furthermore, for each timestep in the time series comes the question of which observation to choose. In the case of optical data, most researchers opt for a time-series with a monthly temporal resolution, choosing the least cloudy product per month [3], [5], [6], [7]. However, a pixel in the tropics and a pixel at high latitude will have different numbers of usable observations, depending on local weather patterns, so the model should be resilient to variable-length, irregularly spaced inputs. In some regions of the world, land observations of certain areas could be consistently underrepresented due to consistent high cloud coverage spanning across the same season over multiple years. Composites offer a pragmatic alternative, distilling an entire period of observations into the memory footprint of a single time-step, as in [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13]. Yet, compositing is not without its own costs: it requires deliberate design choices and non-trivial computations. Typical approaches consist of performing mean or median compositing, the latter involving computing percentiles, and the former being more sensitive to outliers. Moreover, if compositing cannot be performed on-the-fly before downloading the data, practitioners must store (at least temporarily) the time-series the composite will be computed from, undermining much of the storage advantage. While the per-pixel processing cost may appear modest in isolation, it scales dramatically: at a global scale, every additional step must be applied to each pixel on Earth, which can quickly become too costly in many settings. One can also produce a time series of composites, e.g., monthly composites of Sentinel-2 [6], seasonal composites [14], [15], [16], [17], or using a predetermined moving window [4], [18], [19], [20]. Using single time-steps, by contrast, is the most cost-efficient route but comes at the expense of the temporal dimension, which often carries rich, discriminative information. Indeed, Mosig et al. [20] found that performance steadily improved with access to longer input timespans when mapping tree mortality, and Boudras et al. [21] found similar results for canopy height mapping. The consequences of this choice will be felt at every subsequent stage: dataset construction, where samples may or may not share a common shape; model design, where the architecture must be able to represent whatever sampling was chosen; and inference, where every pixel on Earth has to be served the same input structure.
Beyond the choice of temporal representation, the time range itself must be defined. Here, we focus on vegetation-related tasks, for which the trade-offs are particularly well documented, but the same considerations apply across domains. A common default is to restrict the analysis to the leaf-on season [7], [8], [20], [22], [23], [24], but identifying that period for every pixel on Earth is in itself non-trivial. Operational phenology products offer one solution: Mosig et al. [20] use the VIIRS Global Land Surface Phenology product [25], while Liu et al. [23] use the MODIS equivalent [26]. Both products are released at annual intervals, so inter-annual shifts in phenological dates are in principle captured. However, the underlying algorithms assume a vegetation cycle with at most two growing cycles per year, an assumption that breaks down for multi-cropping systems with more than two cycles. Van Tricht et al. [17] bypass this limitation by relying on global crop calendars instead [27], [28]. More fundamentally, the annual leaf-on/leaf-off framing is itself a temperate-zone assumption that does not generalize to tropical systems [29]. The leaf-on framing can also be limiting in its own right: Pauls et al. [3] show that incorporating both summer leaf-on and winter leaf-off observations improves performance, and Karaman et al. [30] find that for biomass estimation in Finland, early-spring Sentinel-2 acquisitions are more informative than summer ones, which they attribute to “the higher contrast between vegetation and snow, which enhances the ability to distinguish vegetation properties”. This logic does not extend everywhere, but regions with strong seasonal contrast can benefit from year-round data. A more task-specific variant samples contrasting images from different times within the same year to expose intra-annual variation, as applied by Kerner et al. [31] for crop field segmentation. The calendar year itself is also a poor natural boundary: for example, in the Southern Hemisphere, summer spans the end of one year and the beginning of the next, so a global-scale pipeline must accommodate such cross-year shifts rather than assume that a single calendar year is a sufficient window. Practitioners therefore need to decide how to balance a simple, globally consistent temporal definition against locally appropriate temporal characterization of the modeled phenomenon.

title: Data selection
text:
Optical data selection
Even after temporal selection, individual observations vary in usability. Two factors dominate optical imagery: cloud contamination and sensor-specific artifacts that introduce gaps or duplications. Rather than discussing the per-pixel quality flags shipped with each product (e.g., the Sentinel-2 SCL band or Landsat QA band), we focus on higher-level quality criteria that govern whether entire products should be included or discarded.
Upon selecting which data product to work with, a common filter in optical imagery is the cloud cover. In the deep learning literature, whether clouds require explicit treatment at all is debated [32], [33], [34]. We argue that this debate, however, does not extend to scene-level selection: a largely obscured acquisition contributes few valid pixels while incurring the full storage cost; filtering acquisitions based on cloud-cover is therefore primarily a question of dataset economy rather than of model robustness. We elaborate on the various methods to perform cloud detection in Data preprocessing and henceforth assume access to a reliable cloud mask. A common approach is to discard data products with a cloud cover above a certain threshold (e.g., 10% in [8], 35% in [35], 60% in [14], 75% in [36], 90% in [31]). However, for regions with persistent cloud cover, naively filtering out entire data products based on their cloud cover percentage induces the risk of throwing away valuable non-cloudy pixels. For example, when compositing, products with high cloud cover may contain cloud-free areas that fill critical gaps in the composite. Alternatives to thresholding differ mainly in the granularity at which they operate. Per-pixel approaches such as Best Available Pixel (BAP) [37], [38] score every observation independently and retain the highest-scoring one at each pixel, so a clear pixel is kept regardless of its parent product’s overall cloud fraction. Product-level approaches instead select a subset of acquisitions: for example, Muhawenayo et al. [36] designed a Sentinel-2 product selection algorithm where products are chosen based on their contribution of valid pixels to under-represented spatial regions within a tile. Which granularity is practical depends in part on where compositing happens. When it can be pushed to the data provider, per-pixel selection is cheap, since rejected observations are never transferred. When data must be retrieved locally, per-pixel scoring requires downloading every candidate acquisition and discarding most of it; selecting a small subset of products becomes the only tractable option. A similar constraint applies to the masks themselves: computing or accessing a cloud mask at the stage of data product selection can be computationally expensive, since it must be done for each candidate product. Most optical data providers report cloud cover statistics in their products metadata, which explains the persistence of scene-level thresholding, despite its known failure mode.






NoteDecision · Selecting optical products based on clouds



Alternatives. Discard whole products above a cloud-cover threshold; compute a mask per candidate and select at pixel level; rank products by their contribution of valid pixels to the area still uncovered.
Trade-off. Product-level thresholds are nearly free, since the statistic ships in the metadata, but they discard cloudy products that may hold the only clear pixels over part of their footprint. Pixel-level selection keeps those pixels and costs a mask computation for every candidate.
Constrains. How many observations survive in persistently cloudy regions; compute available for cloud masks; number of products one can afford to download and store.








NoteRunning example · Cloud screening



WorldCereal did not perform any optical image selection, but masked cloud and shadow (using a variant of the binarized Sen2Cor scene classification mask) prior to compositing.
CHM selected one image per calendar month based on the highest percentage of valid pixels (excluding cloudy and black pixels as identified by the Sen2Cor algorithm). In persistently cloudy regions, the selected image may still be substantially contaminated.


Another important criterion for selecting optical data products is the occurrence of artifacts. For example, Landsat 7 imagery acquired after 2003 exhibits wedge-shaped gaps from the Scan Line Corrector failure, affecting roughly 22% of each scene [39], [40]. More generally, a subtler problem arises when the distribution unit of a product is not aligned with its acquisition unit. Sentinel-2 is the clearest example: the granule is a fixed tile, while the sampling unit is the orbit. Consequently, a tile may be covered partially by one orbit and fully by another, may require mosaicking several orbits acquired on different days, or be affected by other subtle failure cases. Appendix: Identifying Sentinel-2 tiling artifacts illustrates such cases. Addressing these issues is important to avoid duplication of pixel values, which would bias any statistics computed over the data — whether during compositing or when calculating overall dataset statistics from, for example, all Sentinel-2 products acquired within a given time frame, as in [41], [42].

title: Data selection
text:
SAR data selection
SAR imagery is not affected by clouds, but its side-looking acquisition geometry introduces its own artifacts: geometric distortion due to foreshortening, layover, and shadow (see Figure 4.1). These deterministic perturbations arise from the interaction between terrain relief and the radar’s look vector: given a digital elevation model and the acquisition geometry, the distortion pattern can be predicted. This predictability is useful at the selection stage: the sheer data volume and the need for geometric consistency over time argue for working with a subset of the data. Since the distortion associated with each candidate geometry can be computed in advance, that subset can be chosen analytically, before any data is downloaded. Appendix: Selecting a SAR viewing geometry gives an example of this procedure for Sentinel-1.
Another common choice is that of the pass direction. While some regions (among them large portions of Africa, Australia, Russia, Canada and the eastern Americas) are systematically acquired in a single pass direction [43], when both ascending and descending acquisitions of the same area are available, they can be complementary. They should not, however, be treated interchangeably: unless corrected, the azimuthal dependency of \(\sigma^0\) can cause major problems when comparing images acquired from ascending and descending passes [44]. This has a direct impact on model design: global coverage favors models that accept missing modalities (see Model design and training) over ones that assume a complete and fixed input stack.

title: Data preprocessing
text:
SAR preprocessing
Processing steps for Earth observation data vary considerably across the major data sources, but share common goals of converting sensor measurements into analysis-ready data formats. While specific steps differ between optical and SAR, and between missions within each, one constraint governs them all: choices made here shape the distribution of the training data. If any preprocessing choice differs when the model is run at scale, the resulting distribution shift might cause silent failure, with a plausible-looking map. Model evaluation cannot anticipate this; only validating the map against independent reference data can (see Validation). Another related constraint is availability: all processing steps are not available on all platforms. The practical question is therefore not only which processing is theoretically preferable, but which is appropriate enough for the application and available consistently at the scale required.
Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data requires a distinct and often more involved preprocessing chain than optical imagery. SAR sensors measure the coherent backscatter of microwave pulses, and the resulting images are affected by multiplicative speckle noise, radiometric variations driven by local terrain geometry, and geometric distortions inherent to the side-looking acquisition (as described in SAR data selection). Unlike optical sensors, typically delivered as atmospherically corrected products, SAR products such as Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected (GRD) products are distributed at a relatively early processing stage and require several user-side corrections before they can be meaningfully compared across space and time.

title: Data preprocessing
text:
NoteRunning example · Two routes through the speckle decision



WorldCereal filters spatially: a Gamma-MAP filter with a kernel of 7 and three equivalent looks, applied per acquisition and chosen to preserve the original spatial resolution. The series is then composited to 12-day means, with missing values linearly interpolated.
CHM filters temporally: no per-acquisition filter, with quarterly compositing doing the work instead.
What separates both approaches is what each was willing to give up: a little spatial resolution in the first case, the individual acquisitions in the second.



Processing steps
The corrections needed to convert GRD products into analysis-ready backscatter can be grouped into four stages. First, thermal noise removal suppresses additive noise artifacts that are particularly visible near swath edges and in cross-polarization channels. Second, radiometric calibration converts digital numbers to a physically meaningful backscatter coefficient by normalizing by a reference area; the conventions in use (\(\sigma^0\), \(\beta^0\), \(\gamma^0\)) differ in which area they assume, and in whether that area comes from an ellipsoid or from a digital elevation model (see Appendix: Radiometric calibration and terrain correction of SAR data). Third, speckle reduction addresses the multiplicative speckle noise produced by the nature of SAR imaging. Spatial filtering [1], [2], [3] gives up spatial resolution for radiometric smoothness; multi-temporal filtering [4] denoises an image using a stack of acquisitions at higher computational cost, preserving resolution; and temporal averaging, the strategy common in the SatML community [5], [6], preserves spatial detail but discards individual observations. Fourth, geometric and radiometric terrain correction resolves the distortions topography introduces. GRD products are projected onto an Earth ellipsoid and do not account for local relief, so Range-Doppler correction against a DEM is required to recover accurate geolocation, indispensable whenever SAR data is co-located with optical imagery over anything but flat ground. Radiometric terrain correction separately normalizes against the true illuminated area per pixel, without which intensity remains partly a function of slope rather than of ground properties (see SAR data selection). Established toolboxes including pyroSAR [7] and the ESA SNAP toolbox [8] provide implementations of these workflows.


Platform-specific processing
The absence of a standardized preprocessing pipeline for Sentinel-1 GRD data means that the choice of data provider is, in practice, inseparable from the preprocessing approach. Different platforms deliver Sentinel-1 data at different stages of processing, using different DEMs, backscatter conventions, and speckle treatments — differences that can propagate silently into downstream models. Details are provided in Appendix: Sentinel-1 processing across access pathways. Within the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (CDSE) [9], data are available from GRD products to the more recent Sentinel-1 RTC product. Google Earth Engine applies its own processing to native GRD data; the reference implementation [10] and its associated package [11] provide guidance on proper analysis-ready data preparation on GEE. AWS S3 hosts the GRD archive from CDSE in cloud-optimized GeoTIFF format [12] as well as a Sentinel-1 RTC collection over the contiguous United States [13]. Microsoft Planetary Computer [14] provides both a GRD collection from ESA and an RTC collection that they process themselves; for the former, they encourage users to apply geometric or radiometric terrain correction on the fly using any DEM available on the platform. For practitioners that would rather not maintain a SAR processing chain, two products deliver already processed SAR data: the Sentinel-1 Level-3 ARD monthly mosaics (Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem), global at 20m, and the PALSAR/PALSAR-2 yearly mosaics (JAXA), global at 25m. Both are free and both are delivered as terrain-corrected \(\gamma^0\), requiring little user-side preprocessing. We compare them stage by stage in Appendix: Analysis-ready SAR products.






NoteDecision · How much of the SAR chain to perform



Alternatives. Start from GRD and run the four corrections in-house; take a provider’s partially processed product, where thermal noise removal, calibration and terrain correction are applied but speckle is not; or take a finished Level-3 mosaic, where compositing has handled speckle too.
Trade-off. Owning the chain buys control over every convention and keeps individual acquisitions addressable, at the cost of building and maintaining it at scale. Inheriting it buys global consistency produced by people who know the sensor, at the cost of accepting their DEM, their normalization and their compositing rule.
Constrains. Taking a composited product fixes the cadence, so the temporal decision (see Temporal distribution) is made in advance, and orbit direction and incidence angle are no longer selectable, foreclosing the choices discussed in SAR data selection.

title: Data preprocessing
text:
Optical preprocessing
Optical data is typically distributed at two processing levels: top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiance or reflectance, and bottom-of-atmosphere (BOA) reflectance after atmospheric correction. Most ML workflows operate on the latter (Sentinel-2 Level-2A, Landsat Collection 2 Level-2) but several steps remain before the data is ready for model ingestion.

Cloud masking
Cloud and shadow contamination affects all passive optical sensors. Because Sentinel-2 dominates the recent ML literature, most dedicated detection methods have been developed and benchmarked on it. Many such methods transfer to other optical sensors but may require retraining for different bands and resolutions. The available methods range from the Scene Classification Layer shipped with every Sentinel-2 L2A product to dedicated deep learning models, compared in Appendix: Cloud masking methods for optical data. The choice is largely governed by compute: SCL and, for GEE users, Cloud Score+ are already computed, while other methods must be run per product, and the deep learning methods that outperform traditional ones can be substantially more expensive. Furthermore, whether to apply cloud and cloud shadow masking at all depends on the intended use of the data. For workflows that temporally aggregate observations into composites, median aggregation already suppresses most cloud contamination, though masking cloudy and shadowed pixels beforehand generally yields cleaner composites and, for that purpose, the SCL layer is typically sufficient. For workflows that operate on individual scenes, the decision involves a trade-off between input quality and model robustness: aggressive masking produces cleaner inputs but discards data, while retaining cloudy pixels forces the model to learn to identify and handle these artifacts itself, consuming part of its representational capacity.







NoteTry it · Compare cloud masks



The cloud_masks notebook compares tile-level cloud metadata with cloud over an area of interest, contrasts the SCL with Sen2Cor’s cloud probability, and measures what each does to a median composite.





Radiometric conventions
Reflectance is distributed as scaled integers, and the scaling is a convention rather than a constant. Sentinel-2 is a cautionary example: since Processing Baseline 04.00, a radiometric offset is applied to all bands, and because the entire archive was reprocessed in the Collection-1 campaign, the offset must be determined from the PROCESSING_BASELINE metadata field rather than the acquisition date. Some platforms apply the offset upstream, in which case it must not be applied again. The conversion equations and the divisors used in practice are given in Appendix: Radiometric conventions for optical data. The general point is that a scaling convention can change mid-archive, can differ between providers of the same nominal product, and produces no error when applied incorrectly, only a shifted input distribution.


Illumination corrections
Level-2 products still contain systematic reflectance variation unrelated to surface properties. The largest source is viewing and illumination geometry: pixels at swath edge are observed at a different angle than those at nadir, and sun position changes across orbits and dates, so the same ground pixel yields different values purely because of geometry. Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) normalization adjusts reflectance to a standard viewing and illumination configuration, producing smoother time series and reducing visible seam lines at tile boundaries, at the cost of surface structure assumptions and an additional preprocessing step. Implementations are available through Sentinel Hub [15], the sen2nbar package [16] and the FORCE framework [17]. Landsat, and its harmonization with Sentinel-2, is covered in Appendix: Combining Landsat and Sentinel-2.







NoteRunning example · Who performed the preprocessing



WorldCereal ran its own chain. In the first phase, it started from Sentinel-2 L1C on AWS and applied atmospheric correction and cloud masking in-house, because the L2A archive was not yet consistent across the globe, and computed backscatter from Sentinel-1 GRD in the same pass. In the second phase, openEO on CDSE computes backscatter on the fly, but the chain remains theirs to specify.
CHM inherited most of it. Sentinel-1 was taken from Google Earth Engine, which fixes the convention at \(\sigma^0\) and the DEM at SRTM; ALOS PALSAR-2 was taken already terrain-corrected and composited. Only Sentinel-2 was processed from the archive directly.
Neither choice was free. WorldCereal owned the chain because no available product met its consistency requirement; the canopy height group inherited it because running that chain over seven years of global data was not feasible for a university group. Circumstance settled it in both cases, not preference.

title: Machine learning dataset construction and model training
text: With preprocessed data in hand, the focus shifts to the machine learning core of the pipeline. Everything up to this point has concerned analysis-ready data, whereas from here the concern is ML-ready data, in the sense fixed in the “Processing levels, analysis-ready, ML-ready” definition (see Overview of the EO data infrastructure landscape). This section covers two stages: constructing an ML-ready dataset (see Constructing a machine-learning-ready dataset) and designing and training the model (see Model design and training). Each stage raises challenges that are specific to the EO context, and the decisions made at these stages directly determine the quality of the pixel-level predictions.
crumbs: Machine learning dataset construction and model training

title: Constructing a machine-learning-ready dataset
text:
Data formats
Constructing an ML-ready dataset from EO imagery introduces challenges that have no direct analog in standard computer vision: spatial autocorrelation in the labels inflates apparent performance [1], [2] if not handled at the splitting stage, geographic bias in the sampling distorts what the model learns, and the choice of tiling and gridding scheme can silently introduce data leakage or duplication. We address these issues in turn, starting with the data formats that underpin the entire dataset design.
The data format used to store an ML-ready dataset is a creation time decision that propagates through the entire pipeline. It defines how array payloads are physically laid out, how metadata are encoded, how chunks or tiles are addressed, and which codec is required to decode the data. These choices are not strictly irreversible, but changing them requires repacking, rechunking, or rewriting the dataset, and they should therefore be treated as part of the dataset design rather than as a late implementation detail. The most important consequence of a format choice is the efficiency of the access pattern. The optimal layout minimizes over-read, understood as the gap between bytes fetched from storage and bytes actually used by the model. In practice, this depends on how well the physical layout matches the logical access pattern of training, including the shape of the chunks, the band interleaving strategy, the compression block size, the placement of metadata, and the latency of the storage backend. Most formats used for ML on EO data can be understood through three broad storage patterns, summarized in Table 6.1.
crumbs: Machine learning dataset construction and model training

title: Constructing a machine-learning-ready dataset
text:
Container formats with an internal index
The first pattern stores data inside binary containers, each with its own internal metadata and offset structures. HDF5 [3], netCDF-4 [4], GeoTIFF [5], and COG [6] belong to this family. HDF5 (Hierarchical Data Format 5) organizes data as hierarchical groups and arrays, with chunked storage the only layout supporting compression. NetCDF-4 [7] builds on HDF5 while imposing the NetCDF (Network Common Data Form) data model of named variables, dimensions, and attributes, and is usually paired with the Climate and Forecast conventions [8], which enables the comparison of datasets from different sources without ad hoc translation. GeoTIFF (georeferenced TIFF) extends TIFF (Tag Image File Format) with geospatial keys that tie raster coordinates to a coordinate reference system. Unlike HDF5 and netCDF-4, it is fundamentally a two-dimensional raster format, so spectral bands are carried as samples per pixel or as separate images, rather than as axes of an N-dimensional array. COG is a profile of GeoTIFF that constrains this layout for efficient partial reads over HTTP. Two properties govern performance across the family. The first is the order in which array values are serialized, called the interleave (or chunk shape), which fixes which neighbors end up physically adjacent in the file and therefore which reads are cheap. The second is the cost of opening the file. The internal index of offsets and byte lengths must be fetched before any data can be addressed, but once that index sits in memory, reads to individual chunks are independent and parallel by design.


Key-value chunk stores
The second pattern stores arrays as independently addressable chunks in a key-value store, of which Zarr [9] is the canonical example. Each encoded chunk sits under a key in an abstract store, which may be a directory on a filesystem or any backend exposing equivalent read and write operations. This removes the need to open a single monolithic container before locating chunk data, since the storage keys themselves provide the addressing mechanism, which aligns naturally with distributed readers and parallel workloads. The trade-off is that a naive Zarr layout can create very large numbers of small files or objects, which stresses POSIX metadata operations and filesystem inode limits, or inflates object storage request overhead. The Zarr v3 sharding extension (ZEP 2) addresses this by packing multiple logical chunks into a larger physical storage object while preserving chunk level access. Zarr defines array storage, chunking, codecs, and metadata containers, but not the geospatial meaning of coordinates, CRS, or affine transforms, which GeoZarr and related conventions are emerging to supply.

Chunk size is a property of the workload as much as of the format. In one cloud-scale Xarray/Dask analysis of a 250 TB Zarr archive, increasing chunks from about 200 MiB to about 840 MiB shrank the task graph from 1.3 million to about 320,000 tasks and eliminated memory spilling on the workers [10]. 


Columnar tables
The third pattern stores samples as rows rather than arrays as chunks. Not every model consumes patches: for pixel-based algorithms, a table is the natural container. GeoParquet stores samples as rows, features and labels as columns, and the row group rather than the chunk as the unit of access; the geometry column keeps each sample georeferenced. Reading a subset of columns does not require touching the others, which suits feature tables that are wide but sparsely used.

title: Constructing a machine-learning-ready dataset
text:
Dataset splits
When evaluating the performance of an ML model, we want to avoid over-confident results. A conventional uniformly at random assignment of data samples to training and test sets can bias the evaluation if labels are spatially auto-correlated and clustered [11]. A widely spread approach to tackle spatial autocorrelation is to perform block cross-validation, which Roberts et al. [12] recommend using “wherever dependence structures exist in a dataset, even if no correlation structure is visible in the fitted model residuals, or if the fitted models account for such correlations”. Spatial \(K\)-fold block cross-validation first divides the area into non-overlapping spatial blocks of a certain size, before assigning each block to one of \(K\) folds. Model training and evaluation are then performed using the leave-one-fold-out method, where samples from a single fold are set aside for model evaluation, while samples from the remaining \(K-1\) folds are used for model training, and the process is repeated for each fold, as in [13], [14]. Alternatively, one fold can be assigned for model evaluation, one fold for validation, and the \(K-2\) others for training, as in [15]. Results are then reported across the concatenated test folds. In order to avoid cross-fold contamination, a good practice consists in enforcing spatial buffers between blocks, as in [15]. Buffers and block size address the same underlying issue and are partially substitutable: sufficiently large blocks reduce edge leakage to negligible levels without explicit buffers [12], while buffers are most useful when block size is constrained by study extent or sample distribution. We illustrate those different approaches in Figure 6.1. While spatial block cross-validation provides a reliable assessment of model generalizability, most works perform a more limited spatial block validation equivalent to setting \(K=1\), in which blocks are partitioned once and randomly assigned to train, validation, and test sets [16], [17], [18], [19]. The definition of a block varies across works. Some impose a regular grid (Mosig et al. [13] grid the Earth into non-overlapping blocks of 50 km in an equal area projection) while others adopt the geographical unit at which the data is delivered, such as Sentinel-2 tiles [20] or Planet quads [17], [21]. Lusk et al. [14] take a more principled approach, determining the spatial autocorrelation via semivariograms at a \(1\text{km}^2\) resolution and defining hexagonal blocks accordingly. The appropriate block size depends on the spatial scale of residual autocorrelation: blocks should be substantially larger than the distance at which model residuals become uncorrelated, since smaller blocks leave train and test samples near boundaries effectively dependent [12]. We elaborate on various gridding choices and their implications in the next section.






Figure 6.1: Random splits leave train and test points autocorrelated, producing optimistic error estimates (a). Spatial blocks separate folds geographically, but when blocks are not much larger than the range of residual autocorrelation, points near block boundaries remain correlated across folds (b). Adding a buffer zone that excludes near-boundary samples removes this leakage and yields realistic evaluation (c). Equivalently, blocks sized substantially larger than the residual autocorrelation range can achieve realistic evaluation without explicit buffers. The buffered design is most useful when block size is constrained by data extent or sample distribution.



While we have focused on spatial blocking, the underlying principle generalizes to any source of dependence in the data: folds must be independent along whatever structure the model is expected to extrapolate across. Extensions include phylogenetic blocking for taxonomic relatedness [22], temporal blocking for serial autocorrelation [23], and blocking in environmental or feature space, which tests generalization to novel conditions rather than novel locations [24]. The appropriate choice depends on what form of generalization the evaluation is meant to characterize.
Furthermore, in the case of geographically distributed labeled data, it might be of interest to evaluate the performance of the model for different regions, by defining individual splits for each region, as in [18]. This also enables the assessment of a model’s geographical generalization abilities in a comprehensive manner: any region can be held out from the training set and be evaluated on, as in [25].






NoteRunning example · How the two products drew their splits



WorldCereal divides its data randomly into 70% train, 20% validation and 10% test samples, a split that takes no account of spatial structure at all.
CHM holds out one test area of \(960\,\text{m}\times960\,\text{m}\), placed at random inside each Sentinel-2 tile. Every tile therefore contributes both training and test data, and the separation between them rests on a minimum distance of 360 m between training and testing patches.

title: Constructing a machine-learning-ready dataset
text:
Spatial gridding
A map-making pipeline involves not one, but four different grids. The source grid is how the EO data archive is organized; it is inherited, and its seams and overlap are to be dealt with (see Optical data selection). The sampling grid indexes the dataset: it determines which locations become samples, how they are deduplicated, and where the boundaries between training and test data fall. The inference grid partitions the Earth for prediction, and the product grid determines how the finished map is stored and distributed; both are discussed in Map production and distribution. We hereby discuss the second. The three properties compared in Table 6.2 are the ones that matter for sampling: a grid is equal-area if every cell represents the same ground area; conformal if it preserves local angles and shapes, so that a square pixel corresponds to a square patch on the ground; and globally continuous if it covers the Earth without seams or inter-zone overlaps. We group candidate grids into four families, which we now describe.

Geographic grids
Geographic grids partition the Earth by lines of constant latitude and longitude, indexing cells in angular rather than metric units. The simplest instance is plate carrée: cells of fixed angular extent that are trivial to index but whose ground area scales with the cosine of the latitude. A \(1^\circ \times 1^\circ\) cell covers approximately 12,300 km\(^2\) at the equator and about 2000 km\(^2\) at \(80^\circ\) latitude, such that uniform sampling on this grid systematically oversamples high latitudes.


Projection-based tilings
Projection-based tilings lay a regular metric Cartesian grid over a planar coordinate system produced by a general-purpose cartographic projection. The grid’s geometric properties (conformality, area preservation, global continuity) are inherited from the projection. Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) is the industry standard of \(256\times256\) pixel tiles used by web mapping platforms. It is conformal but not equal-area, with ground resolution varying by roughly a factor of six between the equator and \(\pm80^\circ\) latitude. UTM partitions the globe into 60 UTM zones of \(6^\circ\) width, each with a conformal transverse Mercator projection. MGRS [26] subdivides each UTM zone by \(\approx8^\circ\) latitude bands into grid zones, each further divided into 100 km × 100 km squares. The Sentinel-2 tiling scheme, which inherits the UTM/MGRS framework, delivers products as 109.8 km × 109.8 km tiles, such that locations within the resulting ≈10 km border strips appear in two (or more) tiles [27]. The Equi7 Grid [28] uses seven continental sub-grids in Equidistant Azimuthal projections with a multi-level tiling structure (100 km \(\times\) 100 km at level T1), offering a principled alternative to MGRS. A single worldwide plane is simpler still: partitioning an equal-area projection such as Equal Earth (EPSG:8857) into regular cells gives exact equal-area stratification, at the cost of shape distortion toward the poles and a discontinuity at the antimeridian.


Discrete Global Grid Systems (DGGS)
Discrete Global Grid Systems are tessellations of the sphere designed to provide approximately or exactly equal-area cells with global continuity, avoiding the zone boundaries and overlaps of projection-based tilings. S2 Geometry [29] projects the sphere onto a cube and subdivides each face via a quadtree, yielding approximately equal-area quadrilateral cells (area ratio \(\leq 2\) at any level). H3 [30] tiles the sphere in nested hexagons with similar distortion bounds. HEALPix [31] achieves exact equal-area pixelation of the sphere on iso-latitude rings; its rHEALPix variant [32] unfolds the tessellation onto a planar rectangle.


Indexing grids
The three families above all define cells, committing to a geometry before any imagery is read. A fourth approach defines only an index and leaves the geometry to the source. Major TOM [33] defines a set of approximately equidistant sampling points on the WGS84 ellipsoid, adapting longitudinal spacing to latitude so that high latitudes are not oversampled, while prescribing neither projection nor cell extent; patches are extracted in the source product’s native CRS.






NoteDecision · Which grid to sample and split over



Alternatives. A geographic grid, trivial to index but with cell area varying by latitude; a projection-based tiling such as UTM/MGRS, which matches how optical archives are delivered but carries zone seams and tile overlaps; a discrete global grid system, which buys equal-area cells and global continuity at the cost of reprojecting every patch; or an indexing grid that defines no cell at all.
Trade-off. Equal-area cells make sampling density interpretable as labels per unit ground area and make area-based statistics meaningful; conformal, archive-native tilings avoid resampling the imagery. No grid offers both, and the choice is between distorting the sampling or distorting the pixels.
Constrains. A grid whose cells overlap cannot guarantee disjoint splits however the folds are assigned, deduplication has to operate in a common geographic reference rather than on cell identifiers, and uniform sampling over its cells is biased toward the overlaps.

title: Constructing a machine-learning-ready dataset
text:
Data samples
With the data format, splitting strategy, and grid in place, the final step is to extract the actual samples used to train the model. We define a data sample as a \(W\times H\times T \times C\) patch, where \(W\) is the width, \(H\) is the height, \(T\) is the number of time steps, and \(C\) is the number of channels (dimensionality of the EO data at hand). This process involves three considerations: the choice of projection, the sampling strategy, and the optional alignment of the various data modalities.

Sampling strategy
ML researchers typically need to extract EO data samples corresponding to a set of labeled points (or polygons) distributed non-uniformly. In label-scarce regimes, the classic approach is to extract a sample per label, a sampling design that inherits the geographic bias the labels might have. An alternative approach is to sample a certain number of samples per grid cell, keeping all labels in sparsely populated cells and subsampling in densely populated ones, preventing dense regions from dominating. The area that each cell represents impacts the sampling: if the cells have area variation (like S2/H3) or are latitude-distorted (plate carrée), this sampling implicitly gives smaller cells more samples per unit area. For the cap to correspond to a true “labels per \(\text{km}^2\)” ceiling, one can use equal-area grids (HEALPix) or weight by cell area.


Projection choice
The projection in which training samples are processed is a separate decision from the projection in which the finished map is delivered, and the two need not agree. This paragraph concerns the first, and Map production and distribution the second. Most works keep the training data in the native CRS at which it is distributed [13], [19], [20], [34], [35], [36], [37], which for Sentinel-2 is UTM/WGS84. UTM is conformal and holds ground sampling distance near-constant within a zone, so a pixel represents approximately \(10\text{ m}\times 10\text{ m}\) on the ground everywhere within a zone [38] and a patch of fixed pixel dimensions covers a near-constant ground area. Others reproject to a single global CRS such as EPSG:3857 (Web Mercator) [21] or EPSG:4326 [18]. The cost is that the same patch then represents different ground areas at different latitudes, so a model with a fixed receptive field sees a different spatial scale depending on where its training sample came from. If a single global CRS is required, an equal-area projection (e.g., Equal Earth, EPSG:8857) holds that area constant, at the cost of shape distortion.


Multimodal alignment
When training patches combine data from multiple sensors (e.g., Sentinel-2 and ALOS-2 PALSAR-2), the inputs will generally differ in native projection, pixel spacing, and temporal sampling. The most common solution is to reproject and resample all modalities onto a shared grid and resolution before patch extraction, so that each training sample is aligned. This simplifies the data loader and model architecture but forces a choice of target resolution. The choice of resampling kernel also interacts with the downstream task: nearest-neighbor preserves categorical or integer-valued layers but introduces blocky patterns, whereas smooth kernels suit continuous fields but blur edges. An alternative is to preserve each modality at its native resolution and delegate alignment to the model architecture (see Model design and training), avoiding information loss at the cost of greater architectural complexity.
Taken together, these considerations argue for decoupling two concepts that are often conflated: the indexing strategy (how to select samples) and the patch projection (the coordinate system each sample lives in). Indexing should be done on a global grid that minimizes over-/under-sampling and overlap, independently of the patch projection and of how the EO data is tiled. Operations that rely on geography, such as train/test splitting, should be done on this grid. The patch projection, by contrast, only needs to minimize distortion at the scale of a single patch. UTM/WGS84, for instance, is a natural choice when the source archive is already UTM-native.

title: Model design and training
text:
Trade-off
Model design must balance predictive accuracy against inference throughput at continental or global scale, and accommodate the heterogeneity of EO data. Effective model training must examine the specificities of large EO datasets to guide hyperparameter tuning and data augmentation.
Developing ML models for large-scale EO applications requires balancing model complexity, predictive performance, and inference throughput. This trade-off becomes critical in operational settings, where maps must be produced on fixed schedules (quarterly to yearly monitoring) or on demand (real-time alerts, post-disaster response) over wide areas. It is largely shaped by two choices: the model family, and the use of spatial context. Model families range widely in cost. At the simple end, tree ensembles such as gradient boosting and random forests remain common in operational products [1], [2], [3], being cheap to train and deploy without GPUs. At the complex end, Vision Transformer architectures have attracted growing interest, including for large-area mapping [4], [5], [6], [7]. Simpler convolutional encoder-decoder architectures remain widely adopted in operational pipelines, where the latency and memory constraints often favor their lower computational footprint [8], [9], [10]. In particular, UNet architectures [11] with EfficientNet backbones [12] offer a well-documented trade-off between accuracy and throughput for such settings. Most of these architectures operate on image patches, exploiting the spatial context around each pixel. Many operational products instead predict each pixel independently, from its own time series [1], [4], [13], giving up spatial information in exchange for smaller inputs and simpler inference. Knowledge distillation [14] offers a further avenue to improve inference efficiency without notable performance degradation [15].
A recent benchmark of inference throughput across 45 vision backbones and geospatial foundation-model encoders illustrates the stakes: on a single H100 GPU, forward-pass throughput varies by roughly 205× between the fastest and slowest models, whereas moving the same model from a V100 to an H100 yields only a 3–5× speedup. For planetary-scale inference, model choice therefore dominates hardware choice, and combining half precision with torch.compile gives the largest gains [16].

title: Model design and training
text:
Handling input heterogeneity
EO applications frequently combine inputs that differ in spatial resolution, number of channels, or temporal cadence. Rather than resampling all modalities to a common grid before ingestion (as described in From grid to patches), an alternative approach consists in delegating this alignment to the model itself. Typical designs employ modality-specific encoder branches that operate at each source’s native resolution and fuse representations at a shared spatial scale, either through learned upsampling, cross-attention, or feature concatenation after spatial alignment layers [17]. This strategy avoids the interpolation artifacts and information loss inherent in a priori resampling. Recent geospatial foundation models have pushed this flexibility further, using dynamic patch embeddings and scale-adaptive encoders to train a single model across sensors with arbitrary channel counts, resolutions, and tile extents, while also gracefully handling missing or variable modalities at inference time [18], [19], [20]. The added architectural complexity must, however, be weighed against the throughput and simplicity advantages of a single pre-aligned input tensor, particularly in operational pipelines where inference latency is a binding constraint.

title: Model design and training
text:
Hyperparameter tuning
Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is an important step in the ML pipeline, and we refer the reader to [21] for a general review of HPO good practices. We focus on two key aspects that are relevant for large EO datasets: which parameters to optimize, and how much data to use for it. Which parameters matter depends on the model family. Hyperparameter tuning for deep learning models is inherently challenging: the number of configurable hyperparameters is large, and their relative influence on model performance varies across tasks, architectures, and datasets, making it difficult to establish universally valid tuning priorities. Nevertheless, a broad consensus has emerged in the literature that the learning rate and its scheduler, batch size, and regularization mechanisms such as dropout and weight decay tend to be the most influential hyperparameters for deep neural networks [22]. Classical ML models have fewer hyperparameters: for gradient boosting trees, for example, the learning rate is the main one to tune [23]. Regarding how much data should be used for HPO, the common practice is to use the entire validation set, as in [4], [24]. However, given the computational cost of training on large datasets, a strategy encountered in the literature (e.g., [25]) is to perform hyperparameter optimization on a subset of the data, and subsequently train the final model on the full dataset using the selected configuration. This approach is a special case of multi-fidelity hyperparameter optimization, and many methods have been developed for it [26], [27], [28], ranging from simple random subsampling to gradient-based subset selection. When complex subset selection methods are not warranted, stratified random sampling should be preferred over naive uniform sampling, particularly in the presence of class imbalance or long-tailed distributions, to ensure that the subset adequately reflects the class distribution of the original dataset. When using the full dataset is prohibitively expensive, we suggest adopting a two-stage strategy: first using the subset for efficient hyperparameter search to narrow the configuration space, then validation of the top-performing configurations on the full dataset before final model training. We encourage researchers to document their hyperparameter optimization or to report when none was performed, as in [10].

title: Model design and training
text:
Data augmentation
In the SatML field, less attention is brought to data augmentation than in the general ML field. This is partly due to the fact that “augmentation techniques designed for natural images should not be applied to satellite imagery without careful consideration” [29]. Their findings suggest that while standard natural image techniques (particularly color-based augmentations) do not translate effectively to the satellite domain, geometric operations remain a beneficial approach. Furthermore, Muhawenayo et al. [30] have identified that without specific data augmentation techniques to make them resilient, ML models often lack the necessary robustness to handle domain shifts (e.g., in terms of brightness) which can lead to decreased performance and visual artifacts. Various data augmentation techniques have been established in the literature to improve model generalization. Geometric transformations (such as rotations, flips, and random cropping) are being applied to EO data [8], [9], [31], [32], although particular care must be taken for SAR, since the look direction fixes which side of a slope shows layover or shadow. Recent research has introduced domain-specific augmentations tailored to EO data. To enhance spectral robustness, noise is frequently added to Sentinel-2 surface reflectance values [4], [31], while Muhawenayo et al. [30] advocate for varying Sentinel-2 processing strategies to mitigate sensitivity to shifting processing conventions. For models incorporating spatial metadata, Van Tricht et al. [1] apply random perturbations to latitude and longitude coordinates. Furthermore, temporal augmentations, such as dropping timesteps, are utilized to simulate cloud-induced data gaps [4] or missing modalities. Finally, several approaches specifically target sensor-induced artifacts to ensure resilience during inference; these include simulating narrow no-data seams in Sentinel-1 GRD mosaics [33], as well as modeling swath boundaries, misregistration, and detector failures [34].
A model trained with the practices described above will produce a prediction for every pixel on Earth. However, a prediction should come with a measure of its confidence. The model cannot perform equally well everywhere: it will be more reliable in regions well-represented in the training data than in under-sampled biomes, more confident under clear-sky conditions than under persistent cloud cover, and more accurate for common classes than for rare ones. Characterizing where and how much to trust the predictions is the subject of the next section, which surveys ML uncertainty quantification methods and argues that uncertainty is not a supplementary layer to be added as an afterthought, but a necessary component of any credible map product.

title: Uncertainty quantification
text:
International frameworks for climate reporting, including the UNFCCC REDD+ mechanism [1] and IPCC national greenhouse gas inventory guidelines [2], require that participating countries report estimates of forest carbon stock changes with quantified uncertainty. Carbon credit markets depend on this, as overconfident uncertainty bounds can overstate the precision of issued credits, while excessively wide bounds waste verification resources [3]. Beyond carbon accounting, uncertainty is what transforms a map from a static product into a tool that can guide action by identifying where additional field measurements would be most valuable, where policy conclusions are robust, and where they are not.
The challenge is that uncertainty quantification (UQ) for maps is different from UQ for individual predictions. Maps are spatial products, so users do not consume pixel values in isolation but aggregate them into regional statistics, compare them across years, and derive change estimates. A model may be well-calibrated on average across a global test set while being systematically overconfident in specific biomes or regions. If the uncertainty layer does not capture this spatial variation in reliability, it fails where it is most needed.
This section surveys the methods available for quantifying prediction uncertainty in large-scale EO maps, the techniques for assessing whether that uncertainty is trustworthy, the underappreciated role of spatial error correlation in aggregated estimates, and the practical question of what to do with uncertainty once it has been estimated.
Throughout, we distinguish two branches of large-scale mapping that differ in what an uncertainty estimate is. For continuous targets (biomass, canopy height, soil properties) uncertainty is a predictive distribution or interval around a real-valued prediction, and calibration is assessed by whether intervals achieve their nominal coverage. For categorical targets (land cover, crop type, change detection) uncertainty is a probability vector over classes, and calibration is assessed by whether those probabilities match observed class frequencies. The two branches share most of the method families below but not all of them, and they have different validation methods. Categorical mapping has a design-based tradition for aggregate accuracy and area estimation [4], [5] but comparatively weak per-pixel uncertainty products, whereas continuous mapping has invested in per-pixel uncertainty but has only recently begun to address the aggregate problem (see Spatial structure of uncertainty). We note where method applications diverge as we go.

title: Sources of uncertainty
text:
Upstream (input) uncertainty
The total uncertainty in a map prediction arises from multiple, largely independent sources that are usefully organized into the classical distinction between aleatoric uncertainty (irreducible noise inherent in the data) and epistemic uncertainty (reducible uncertainty arising from limited knowledge) [1]. In the context of EO-derived maps, however, this abstract distinction maps onto pipeline stages.
Every observation that enters the model carries errors introduced before any machine learning is applied. Sensor noise, imperfect atmospheric correction, cloud mask failures, co-registration errors between sensors, compositing artifacts, and BRDF effects all contribute. These sources are predominantly aleatoric at the pixel level though the magnitude of the noise varies spatially (e.g., atmospheric correction is harder over bright surfaces) and can therefore appear epistemic at the map level. In principle, one would propagate input uncertainty through the model via Monte Carlo simulation over perturbed inputs [2]. In practice, this is rarely done since the computational cost is substantial, and the input uncertainty distributions are themselves poorly characterized. Nevertheless, it is important to acknowledge that model-derived uncertainty is only one component of the total error.

title: Sources of uncertainty
text:
Label (reference data) uncertainty
The training targets are themselves uncertain. For example, GEDI footprint-level AGBD estimates carry uncertainty from allometric models and instrument noise [3], national forest inventory plots carry measurement error and representativeness uncertainty, and crowdsourced labels carry annotator disagreement. Label noise is a form of aleatoric uncertainty that sets a floor on achievable prediction accuracy. Methods that assume noise-free labels, which are most standard loss functions, will conflate label noise with model error in their uncertainty estimates.

title: Sources of uncertainty
text:
Model (epistemic) uncertainty
This encompasses everything the model does not know such as gaps in the training data distribution, misspecification of the functional form, and sensitivity to hyperparameter choices. Model uncertainty is highest where the inference domain differs from the training domain, which is exactly the regime that matters for global maps, which inevitably extrapolate beyond the spatial and temporal extent of their training data.
Many UQ methods address only model uncertainty. The gap between what is quantified and what contributes to the total error budget should be made explicit.
